chapter: Philadelphia, Detroit and back to Atlantic City
title: Jake Gillum's Madhouse in Philadelphia
summary: He describes his job at the Madhouse, a confusing rough place with prizefighter waiters, which he regained after the war.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Cabarets, honky-tonks and the Storyville nightlife scene

blocks.x: See, before I left, I told you, the last days of '18, before we went in, the beginning of '18, the last days of '17, rather, I worked in the -- had a job in Philadelphia at a place called the Madhouse. Jake Gillum's Madhouse, it was Jessup and Poplar Streets in Philadelphia. Cause I wanted to be home, see. And in being there, so when I went to war, I come out and went back there to see Jake Gillum, and ask him, "Well, I've just been in the war, and could I get my job back." And he said, "Well, sure, anytime a man goes over there for his country, he should have his job back." So he gave me this job back. Now this is my first organization of having an outfit together that would sound something like a band.
I see. But let's go back, then, because you were at the Madhouse before you went into the service.
What was the Madhouse like? What did it look like, and what kind of people were there, music and --
The only way I can explain that is, "confusion".

Yeah. It was almost as bad as the Bucket of Blood, but it was one step higher. But it was confusion. And, well I can tell you one thing about the Madhouse. Well, we did an awful lot of -- we played for a lot of people there, and they liked us very much. Because -- but, one thing about it was that

when you come into the Madhouse, every waiter on the floor was a prizefighter. All one punch men. And, when they used to throw you out, Jake, being a very good politician, they come to lock you up for disturbing the peace. And you hadn't done anything. That was the way of doing things.

But, one thing, you had a chance, you had plenty of entertainers there. And I really learnt more about playing for singers, because, singers -- and they had plenty of them coming in there, and they were liable to sing in any key. Sometimes one of the would come in to sing and it's A, and another one B, and E, and another one would be in E-flat. And so, you got something that the kids nowadays cannot get, unless they're way down in Virginia someplace or in North Carolina. Because here there's no place on that lower status now. Everything is built up, so they lose that experience. They'll never get it.
